newsitem.title: UK: LME enjoys up-beat day but ends off its best.
newsitem.headline: LME enjoys up-beat day but ends off its best.

text.p: Base metal markets largely traded in the plus column on Wednesday, with LME copper leading the way, although the pace of trading was slow and most markets closed off their highs.
Traders said mid-afternoon levels of $2,600 and $1,600 respectively for copper and aluminium proved unsustainable, and both contracts fell back towards the kerb close.
"I think they tried the figure in both cases, did not like the air up there, which was unsurprising, and just came back. There was a bit of spec selling on copper, but nothing big," one trader said.
Copper's failure to break above $2,600 was well-signposted, with the market perhaps still overbought and some heavy resistance expected around $2,610 and above.

However, the spread backwardation flipped out above $100, basis cash/threes, underlining continued technical tightness which flares up on certain dates, and this should keep the market underpinned, analysts said.
Final three months business on the kerb was at $2,592 a tonne, up $10 from Tuesday's close.

Aluminium dutifully followed copper higher, but lacked real independent momentum and never looked like regaining levels above $1,600. Stocks continue to decline - down another 3,100 tonnes - but this is having little impact on prices.
Last business was at $1,593, still up $9 with the market likely to range-trade between $1,570 and $1,600 in the short-term, traders said.
Nickel business was mostly low-key throughout, with little movement seen after an initial flip-up above $7,200, and the market closed at $7,230, a gain of $20.
Traders said short-term direction continues to be influenced by the Inco, Sudbury strike and Norilsk's gas power dispute, and there have been no fresh developments in either case.
Zinc flipped up to the highs of a tight day's trading range on the kerb in short-covering, building on the earlier trade buying. Last business was at $1,375, up $7 from Tuesday.
Lead continued to correct up from yesterday's 20-month lows, with some trade interest also seen, although the extent of the upmove was restricted. Prices closed with modest $2 gains at $624.
The tin market similarly steadied in tandem with the rest of the complex, but remains vulnerable to a re-test of recent one-year lows at $5,510. Last trade was at $5,580, up just $10.
Alloy was steadier when traded today, and closed at $1,472/75 a tonne, up from the previous close of $1,465.
